Infections of the mucosa of the respiratory tract or gastrointestinal tract, or of abraded skin, usually with Rhiz- opus or Rhizomucor spp., can result in local invasion of deeper tissues including bone and the CNS, with extensive tissue destruction. Disseminated disease may also occur. The treatment of mucormycosis includes a combination of antifungal therapy, surgical debridement when possible, and management of the underlying disease. The standard antifungal therapy is relatively high doses of intravenous amphotericin B or lipid formulations of amphotericin B. Fluconazole, itraconazole, ketoconazole, voriconazole, or the echinocandins are not considered to have a role in the treatment of mucormycosis, although the newer triazoles, posaconazole and ravuconazole, have reported in-vitro ac- tivity against zygomycetes and posaconazole has been tried in patients with refractory disease. Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis 2006; 25: 215–29. Mycetoma Mycetoma1-4 has a worldwide distribution, but is most commonly encountered in the tropics and subtropics. It may affect subcutaneous tissue, bone, and skin. The foot is most often affected (70 to 80% of cases), less often hand (12%), legs, and knee joints. The term Madura foot is used for mycetoma affecting the foot. Infection mainly results from trauma to the skin, and may spread locally through the lymphatic system to surrounding tissues, progressively destroying connective tissue and bone. Mycetomas caused by fungi such as Madurella mycetomatis, M. grisea, or Pseudallescheria boydii are called eumycetomas.
